title: The King No One Can Date

title_i18n.en: The King No One Can Date

subtitle: Simuka, Kanha and the birth of a Deccan dynasty from shards of stone
era: Early Satavahana foundations, c. 120-70 BCE, with debated long and short chronologies
region: Kanaganahalli, Naneghat, Nashik and the western Deccan
moral: Honest history begins by naming uncertainty.

sources.citation: Naneghat cave inscription, published by Georg Buhler in Epigraphia Indica Vol. 4 (1883)
sources.note: Dynastic genealogy naming early Satavahana rulers.

sources.citation: Kanha's Nashik Cave 19 inscription, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 7 (1903-04)
sources.note: Early royal record and Buddhist cave donation using Mauryan administrative vocabulary.

sources.citation: Ajay Mitra Shastri, The Satavahanas and the Western Ksatrapas (1998); Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (2017)
sources.note: Modern discussion of Simuka, Kanaganahalli and the chronology problem.

panels.shot: epic wide of a rocky Deccan plateau dotted with stupas and caves, Simuka and Kanha ghost-like behind carved stones

dialogue.text: In an age of fading Mauryas and rising Saka storms, two brothers—Simuka and Kanha—leave so faint a trail that even today, no one can date their throne.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a scholar’s hand brushing dust from an inscription in a cave

dialogue.text: The story begins not with a court poet, but with dust and stone in a wind-cut pass called Naneghat, where a long, careful inscription whispers a broken family tree.

panels.shot: overhead view of Naneghat pass with traders, then subtle overlay of letters naming kings

dialogue.text: Here, in a cave above the toll-road of Naneghat, a queen carved the Satavahana line: kings, queens and princes, including a founder whose very name shifts like mist between scripts.

panels.shot: close-up on a palm-leaf manuscript of a Purana beside a printed modern book

dialogue.text: Centuries later, the Puranas would call this first king Shishuka, Sipraka, Sindhuka. Their lists stretch and twist his reign, tying him to Kanva kings he never knew.

panels.shot: dramatic split-screen style: on one side a shadowy tyrant of Jain story, on the other a calm, uncertain outline

dialogue.text: Jain storytellers would later paint him as a tyrant toppled by righteous rebels. But the stones of the Deccan stay quiet. They give us a name, not a monster.

panels.shot: low-angle on Simuka standing on a rocky outcrop overlooking the Deccan, hazy Mauryan pillars crumbling behind him

dialogue.text: What we can see is the age. Mauryan power has thinned. Local chiefs rise and fall. From this rough plateau, a man later called Simuka gathers clan and coin, watching both Magadha and Saka frontiers.

panels.shot: medium shot of Simuka in a modest court, consulting with Kanha and elders

dialogue.text: We hold the passes. The caravans need us, not distant kings.

panels.shot: wide shot of Kanaganahalli stupa complex under construction, with artisans at work

dialogue.text: Far to the south-east, beside the Krishna at Kanaganahalli, another trail appears centuries later. Broken slabs show portraits and labels: Siri Chimuka Satavahana… Year 16.

panels.shot: close-up of a Kanaganahalli sculpted slab labelled Siri Chimuka, his figure half-broken

dialogue.text: Here, the founder steps into the light as Siri Chimuka Satavahana—Simuka in another tongue. A real portrait, a regnal year, but still no firm birth or coronation date.

panels.shot: map-like bird’s-eye of western Deccan highlighting Naneghat, Nashik, Kanaganahalli

dialogue.text: Join the dots: Naneghat’s genealogy, Kanaganahalli’s Year 16 slab, coins scattered across the Godavari and Krishna. A dynasty emerges, not in one inscription, but in a web.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of Simuka aging, handing a royal emblem to Kanha

dialogue.text: One by one, the Puranas and Naneghat agree on one thing: after Simuka comes Kanha. Brother follows brother, and the house of Satavahana remains in family hands.

panels.shot: low-angle of Kanha leading an entourage toward a rocky hill that will be Nashik caves

dialogue.text: Kanha steps out not in myth but in his own words, at a rocky outcrop near Nashik, where caves bite into the cliff and the language of Ashoka still lingers in the air.

panels.shot: close-up inside Nashik Cave 19 as a royal officer chisels Kanha’s inscription

dialogue.text: In Cave 19, Kanha’s record calls him raja, uses Mauryan words for offices and provinces, and marks a donation to the Buddha’s community. A new power wears old administrative clothes.

panels.shot: medium on the monk and Kanha exchanging a respectful gesture at the cave entrance

dialogue.text: Let these caves shelter your monks, and our name shelter this land.

panels.shot: interior scholarly shot: modern historians debating with maps and timelines behind

dialogue.text: Yet the question that haunts every seminar remains: did Simuka rise in the shadow of Ashoka, or a century and more later, as Saka Kshatrapas pressed the western coast?

panels.shot: split panel comparing long and short chronologies visually as two diverging timelines

dialogue.text: The old long chronology pushed him back into the 3rd century BCE, tied to Kanvas. New readings from Kanaganahalli pull him forward, towards a late 2nd to early 1st century BCE horizon.

panels.shot: soft-focus vision of Simuka and Kanha fading into a line of later Satavahana rulers

dialogue.text: What matters is clear even through the haze. Simuka and Kanha turn a clan into a state, a plateau into a realm, laying the ground for kings like Satakarni to come.

panels.shot: return to the ancient stones: close-up of Kanaganahalli and Nashik inscriptions side by side

dialogue.text: Between Naneghat, Nashik and Kanaganahalli, the dates narrow, the titles align, the language shifts. But gaps remain, and the honest historian leaves them open instead of filling them with stories.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide: Simuka and Kanha as silhouettes carved in stone, half in light, half in shadow

dialogue.text: Simuka and Kanha remind us that the past is not a neat list but a broken inscription: to honour them is to read what survives, admit what does not, and let uncertainty be part of the truth.
